candidates.title: Map resume facts into application fields

demandEvidence.chore: Manually re-enter resume facts into forms tailored to individual hiring processes.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: I spent two hours every day filling my resume data to freshly developed forms made specifically to the hiring process of one or two companies.

ease.reason: A schema-based extractor supports mapping supplied text to named fields, but form handling is manual.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: job seekers may value less repetitive entry; this post shows no buying intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week synthetic test can map supplied resume facts to operator-provided fields; form variation remains untested.

autonomy.reason: Field suggestions can repeat, but a person must verify and enter every answer.

evidence.reason: The post directly reports repeated resume entry for one or two companies; no field examples or corroboration are supplied.

experimentPlan.output: Produce a reviewable table matching supplied resume facts to user-entered application fields.
inputs: A small set of fictional application questions
experimentPlan.trigger: A user supplies a resume excerpt and a new set of form labels.
steps: Extract candidate facts from the supplied text.
Map each requested field to a matching fact or mark it unknown.
Show the source phrase beside each suggested answer.
Ask the user to review and copy approved values manually.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: Check that every suggested value matches a literal source phrase and that unsupported fields are marked unknown.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: The job seeker supplies their own information, verifies every answer, and submits applications themselves.
unverified: No browser form filling or live application access is documented

candidates.reason: Below threshold: a useful synthetic mapping test is scoped, and the supplied Information Extractor schema docs support structured extraction, but buyer evidence and live form capability are absent.

candidates.title: Prototype salon booking safeguards

demandEvidence.chore: Check each salon booking request against working hours, provider availability, and existing appointments before confirming.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Every booking request checks salon working hours, master availability, and existing appointments in PostgreSQL at the SQL level before confirmation.

ease.reason: The post describes an n8n and PostgreSQL architecture, but no supplied building reference documents its setup.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: beauty salons may pay for booking safeguards; this architecture post establishes no buyer intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week synthetic booking mock is bounded; live calendar integration and concurrency safety remain unverified.

autonomy.reason: A proposed request-to-check loop can repeat, but a person must validate records and approve confirmations.

evidence.reason: The retained spans describe calendar validation and a booking architecture; omitted body context is not assessed.

experimentPlan.output: Return a proposed booking slot as available, unavailable, or needs human review.
inputs: Fictional booking request with date and service
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator submits a fictional booking request for a test salon.
steps: Read the requested date, time, and service from operator-entered fields.
Compare the requested time with the fictional working-hours table.
Check provider availability and overlapping fictional appointments.
Return a status and the specific check that caused it.
Have an operator review the result before any customer confirmation.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: Run cases for an open slot, closed hours, unavailable provider, and overlapping appointment; each result must match the fixture tables.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A salon operator supplies and verifies the test schedule and approves every real booking and customer message.
unverified: No supplied implementation reference supports n8n execution or PostgreSQL persistence
Concurrency behavior in a real booking system
Real calendar permissions and customer data safeguards

candidates.reason: Below threshold: the post documents a concrete booking validation loop, but no supplied reference supports implementation and the source does not establish buyers or demand beyond the maker example.

candidates.title: Review a daily new-job alert loop

demandEvidence.chore: Check selected company career pages daily for new job postings and alert an operator when results appear.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Workflow: Schedule Trigger (daily) → Apify node (“Run an Actor and get dataset”) → IF item count > 0 → Slack.

ease.reason: The retained post demonstrates a schedule, actor result check, and Slack alert; the Summarize docs support counts only, not scraping.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: recruiters or job seekers might pay for monitored job alerts; this maker post shows no buyer demand.

feasibility.reason: A four-week mock can compare fictional daily postings and prepare alerts; live career-site access and freshness remain unverified.

autonomy.reason: A daily check-and-alert loop is described, but a person must verify relevance and the source sites.

evidence.reason: The post gives a specific daily workflow and deduplication claim by its author; independent demand evidence is absent.

experimentPlan.output: Produce a daily review list of newly observed postings from a small operator-maintained test set.
inputs: Synthetic posting rows with title, location, and URL
experimentPlan.trigger: A scheduled mock run receives the latest synthetic posting rows.
steps: Compare each row with the prior-day fixture using its URL.
Mark unseen rows as new and previously seen rows as existing.
Count new rows using the documented Summarize node capability.
Prepare a Slack-style alert draft only when new rows exist.
Have an operator verify each posting before acting on it.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: Check a fixture with one new and one repeated URL; the new count and alert draft must identify only the unseen posting.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: An operator supplies company sources, reviews each posting, and decides whether to contact or apply.
unverified: The supplied Summarize reference documents counting only, not scraping or scheduling
Career-site access, actor reliability, and live Slack delivery
The post is a maker workflow, not evidence of paying alert customers

candidates.reason: Below threshold: the example documents a repeatable hiring alert workflow, but it is a maker post and the supplied building reference supports only counting, not the retrieval workflow or buyer demand.
